newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal public sector wage round runs into snags.
newsitem.headline: Portugal public sector wage round runs into snags.

text.p: Portugal's top public sector trade union official on Wednesday called the government's latest offer to raise wages by 2.6 percent in 1997 unacceptable and said he had called a protest march next month.
"We do not accept this proposal," Carlos Mamede, head of the 300,000-strong Frente Comum, said.
"The government is not including productivity in its proposal and is giving no reasons," he added in a telephone interview. "For us, productivity is important."
Frente Comum represents about half of Portugal's estimated 500,000 to 800,000 civil servants.

Mamede said the government's latest offer in the 1997 public sector wages round did not account for the fact that Portuguese civil servants were paid much less than the average of their colleagues elsewhere in Europe.
He said the state had failed to respond to union demands to erase the differential between the national and public sector minimum wage in Portugal.
The public sector minimum wage was 4.5 percent below the national level of 54,600 escudos ($353) a month, he added.
The government's latest pay offer followed its earlier proposal to raise wages by 2.375 percent, the mid-point between the inflation target for 1997 of between 2.25 and 2.50 percent.
The Socialist government has forecast that inflation will stand at 3.25 percent at the end of 1996. In 1996 the government and public sector unions agreed a 4.25 percent wages increase.

"We can't be sure that the government will meet its inflation targets," Mamede said. "It is not certain that 2.6 percent would be enough to give civil servants a real increase in their salaries," he added.
He said the government had not taken account of real falls in civil servants' purchasing power in recent years.
Mamede said he had called a protest march by civil servants for December 5 in Lisbon and he expected thousands to take part.

Government officials have insisted that public sector wages must be contained in 1997 in order to restrain inflation and boost Portugal's chances of qualifying to join a European single currency in 1999.

Bank of Portugal governor Antonio de Sousa said in a press interview last month that he believed union wage demands were too high and that a one percent differential above inflation should be the maximum acceptable level.

Frente Comum, linked to the Communist-dominated General Confederation of Portuguese Workers (CGTP), has demanded a seven percent increase in the 1997 public sector wages round that began on October 9.
The two other union groups taking part in the talks have demanded a 4.5 percent increase.
Mamede said the next session of talks with the government would take place before the final vote on the 1997 budget in parliament on December 11, but no precise date had been set.
"We want a successful agreement, but the terms have to be right," he said.
